          Liverpool's Evolution: From Survival Mode to WSL Top-Four Contenders
        
      
                          
                      Sep 24, 2026
          
                      Maya Shah / Author, Jakob Abrahamson / Design
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
Are Liverpool genuine top-four contenders in the WSL? We look at the transformation behind their impressive start, the performance that almost earned them a result against Man City, and how their players are helping to drive renewed hope.
Just four months ago, the idea of Liverpool challenging for a UEFA Women's Champions League place would have seemed improbable.
The Reds finished 11th in the Women's Super League in 2025-26, ending the season eight points clear of bottom-placed Leicester City but recording their second-lowest finish in the competition.
Their 2025-26 campaign began in disastrous fashion under the former Manchester City boss Gareth Taylor, as the Reds failed to win any of their opening 12 league matches (D4 L8).
A six-game losing streak at the start of the season set the tone, including an opening weekend loss to rivals Everton at Anfield (4-1) followed by a shock defeat at Leicester City on MD2.
Liverpool found themselves rooted to the foot of the table across the winter break with just three points collected, and facing serious questions about their future direction.
Their struggles continued into the start of 2026 as Liverpool's winless league run reached 15 matches, the longest in their WSL history.
Yet, even amid the poor results, there were signs they could compete.

During that difficult run, Liverpool lost to both Arsenal and Man City by just a single-goal margin, with both winning goals coming in the final four minutes. It was enough to suggest that the gap to the league's elite was not quite as wide as the table implied.
There were also off-field circumstances surrounding the club that cannot be ignored when looking back at Liverpool's 2025-26 WSL campaign.

The passing of former manager Matt Beard in September 2025 cast a shadow over the season. Beard was one of the most influential figures in the club's history, overseeing 106 WSL matches across two spells and guiding them to back-to-back league titles in 2013 and 2014. Against that backdrop, Liverpool's struggles became easier to contextualise.
Taylor’s first WSL victory with the Reds came at home against Tottenham in January, and while Liverpool won only three more league matches across the campaign, it proved enough to secure survival.
Now, less than a year later, the picture looks very different.

Liverpool began 2026-27 with a convincing 4-0 victory over Charlton Athletic, their first win in a season opener since 2023. The four-goal margin was also their biggest in a WSL match since a 4-0 victory over Leicester in May 2024.

They followed that with a 1-1 draw against Tottenham on MD2, a result that arguably failed to reflect the balance of play, before pushing Man City all the way on MD3. An unfortunate 89th-minute own goal by Grace Fisk ultimately denied Liverpool what would have been their first point against City since May 2023.

Results alone, however, only tell part of the story. The underlying numbers point to a Liverpool side that are playing with greater ambition than we saw for much of last season. They are pressing higher, spending more time in possession, and showing a greater willingness to take the game to their opponents rather than simply react to them.

Of course, there are still areas to improve, but the early season data suggests a meaningful shift in Liverpool’s approach. A side that spent much of last season battling at the bottom end of the table are showing signs of being better equipped to compete with the division’s leading teams.
So, can Liverpool turn that promising start into a genuine push for a top-four finish?
They may have left Manchester empty-handed on Friday night, but Liverpool's performance arguably told a more encouraging story than the result itself.

Too often in recent seasons have meetings with the WSL's elite been exercises in damage limitation. Liverpool's approach at the Joie Stadium was markedly different. They pressed aggressively, played through City's pressure and repeatedly forced the hosts into uncomfortable situations.
